tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name: Generate Blog Post

on:
  schedule:
    # Daily at 8:00 AM UTC. The duplicate/mis-title problems that once
    # justified a 3x/week cadence are now caught by the pipeline's hard
    # duplicate guard, H1 title reconciliation, and the CI content tests,
    # so daily drafting is safe again.
    - cron: '0 8 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      mode:
        description: 'Generation mode'
        required: true
        default: 'auto'
        type: choice
        options:
          - auto
          - topic
          - git
      topic:
        description: 'Topic (required when mode is "topic")'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

# Avoid two scheduled runs and a manual dispatch racing each other into
# duplicate PRs against `master`.
concurrency:
  group: blog-post-generator
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  generate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      # Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs so a moved/compromised tag
      # can't inject code into a workflow that holds `contents: write`.
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # full history for git-log mode

      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Generate blog post draft
        env:
          GEMINI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GEMINI_API_KEY }}
          GEMINI_MODEL: 'gemini-2.5-flash'
          INPUT_MODE: ${{ github.event.inputs.mode || 'auto' }}
          INPUT_TOPIC: ${{ github.event.inputs.topic || '' }}
        run: |
          case "$INPUT_MODE" in
            auto|topic|git) ;;
            *) echo "Invalid mode: $INPUT_MODE" >&2; exit 1 ;;
          esac

          if [ "$INPUT_MODE" = "topic" ] && [ -n "$INPUT_TOPIC" ]; then
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js topic "$INPUT_TOPIC"
          else
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js "$INPUT_MODE"
          fi

      - name: Check for new draft
        id: check
        run: |
          if git status --porcelain | grep -q 'blog-src/src/content/posts/'; then
            DRAFT_FILE=$(git status --porcelain | grep 'blog-src/src/content/posts/' | awk '{print $2}' | head -1)
            # Title is AI-generated; never interpolate it directly into a shell command.
            # Sanitize aggressively (printable ASCII minus shell metacharacters) and cap length.
            RAW_TITLE=$(head -5 "$DRAFT_FILE" | grep '^title:' | sed 's/^title: *"//;s/"$//')
            SAFE_TITLE=$(printf '%s' "$RAW_TITLE" | tr -cd 'A-Za-z0-9 _.,:!?-' | head -c 120)
            {
              echo "has_draft=true"
              echo "draft_file=$DRAFT_FILE"
              echo "title=$SAFE_TITLE"
            } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "has_draft=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "No new draft was generated."
          fi

      - name: Create PR with draft
        if: steps.check.outputs.has_draft == 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          DRAFT_TITLE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.title }}
          DRAFT_FILE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.draft_file }}
        run: |
          DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
          SLUG=$(printf '%s' "$DRAFT_TITLE" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -cs 'a-z0-9' '-' | head -c 40)
          BRANCH="blog/draft-${DATE}-${SLUG}"

          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"

          git checkout -b "$BRANCH"
          git add blog-src/src/content/posts/
          git commit -m "draft: $DRAFT_TITLE"
          git push -u origin "$BRANCH"

          gh label create blog-draft --color "0E8A16" --description "Auto-generated blog draft" 2>/dev/null || true

          PR_BODY=$(cat <<EOF
          ## Auto-Generated Blog Draft

          **File:** \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`

          This post was automatically generated by the daily blog pipeline using Google Gemini.

          ### To publish:
          1. Review and edit the post in \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`
          2. Add appropriate tags in the frontmatter
          3. Merge this PR

          > **Note:** The post is written directly into \`posts/\`, so merging this PR
          > publishes and deploys it to the site. Close the PR without merging to discard.

          *Generated via GitHub Actions*
          EOF
          )

          gh pr create \
            --title "📝 Blog Draft: $DRAFT_TITLE" \
            --body "$PR_BODY" \
            --label "blog-draft" \
            --base master

name: Generate Blog Post

on:
  schedule:
    # Daily at 8:00 AM UTC. The duplicate/mis-title problems that once
    # justified a 3x/week cadence are now caught by the pipeline's hard
    # duplicate guard, H1 title reconciliation, and the CI content tests,
    # so daily drafting is safe again.
    - cron: '0 8 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      mode:
        description: 'Generation mode'
        required: true
        default: 'auto'
        type: choice
        options:
          - auto
          - topic
          - git
      topic:
        description: 'Topic (required when mode is "topic")'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

# Avoid two scheduled runs and a manual dispatch racing each other into
# duplicate PRs against `master`.
concurrency:
  group: blog-post-generator
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  generate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      # Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs so a moved/compromised tag
      # can't inject code into a workflow that holds `contents: write`.
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # full history for git-log mode

      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Generate blog post draft
        env:
          GEMINI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GEMINI_API_KEY }}
          GEMINI_MODEL: 'gemini-2.5-flash'
          INPUT_MODE: ${{ github.event.inputs.mode || 'auto' }}
          INPUT_TOPIC: ${{ github.event.inputs.topic || '' }}
        run: |
          case "$INPUT_MODE" in
            auto|topic|git) ;;
            *) echo "Invalid mode: $INPUT_MODE" >&2; exit 1 ;;
          esac

          if [ "$INPUT_MODE" = "topic" ] && [ -n "$INPUT_TOPIC" ]; then
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js topic "$INPUT_TOPIC"
          else
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js "$INPUT_MODE"
          fi

      - name: Check for new draft
        id: check
        run: |
          if git status --porcelain | grep -q 'blog-src/src/content/posts/'; then
            DRAFT_FILE=$(git status --porcelain | grep 'blog-src/src/content/posts/' | awk '{print $2}' | head -1)
            # Title is AI-generated; never interpolate it directly into a shell command.
            # Sanitize aggressively (printable ASCII minus shell metacharacters) and cap length.
            RAW_TITLE=$(head -5 "$DRAFT_FILE" | grep '^title:' | sed 's/^title: *"//;s/"$//')
            SAFE_TITLE=$(printf '%s' "$RAW_TITLE" | tr -cd 'A-Za-z0-9 _.,:!?-' | head -c 120)
            {
              echo "has_draft=true"
              echo "draft_file=$DRAFT_FILE"
              echo "title=$SAFE_TITLE"
            } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "has_draft=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "No new draft was generated."
          fi

      - name: Create PR with draft
        if: steps.check.outputs.has_draft == 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          DRAFT_TITLE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.title }}
          DRAFT_FILE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.draft_file }}
        run: |
          DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
          SLUG=$(printf '%s' "$DRAFT_TITLE" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -cs 'a-z0-9' '-' | head -c 40)
          BRANCH="blog/draft-${DATE}-${SLUG}"

          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"

          git checkout -b "$BRANCH"
          git add blog-src/src/content/posts/
          git commit -m "draft: $DRAFT_TITLE"
          git push -u origin "$BRANCH"

          gh label create blog-draft --color "0E8A16" --description "Auto-generated blog draft" 2>/dev/null || true

          PR_BODY=$(cat <<EOF
          ## Auto-Generated Blog Draft

          **File:** \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`

          This post was automatically generated by the daily blog pipeline using Google Gemini.

          ### To publish:
          1. Review and edit the post in \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`
          2. Add appropriate tags in the frontmatter
          3. Merge this PR

          > **Note:** The post is written directly into \`posts/\`, so merging this PR
          > publishes and deploys it to the site. Close the PR without merging to discard.

          *Generated via GitHub Actions*
          EOF
          )

          gh pr create \
            --title "📝 Blog Draft: $DRAFT_TITLE" \
            --body "$PR_BODY" \
            --label "blog-draft" \
            --base master

I've made the code fixes, but I still need your help with one thing before I change any model names.

**Why the run failed** (scheduled run 35346314572, today):
1. `gemini-2.5-flash` returned 503 (overloaded) three times, so the script moved on to the next model in its fallback list.
2. That fallback, `gemini-2.0-flash`, has been retired. Google now returns a 404: *"This model models/gemini-2.0-flash is no longer available. Please update your code to use models/gemini-3.6-flash."*
3. **This is the actual bug:** `scripts/generate-post-gemini.js` stops the whole run on any error it doesn't retry, and a 404 is one of those. So the third model, `gemini-2.5-flash-lite`, was never tried.
4. Separately, the embedding model `text-embedding-004` also 404s now. That doesn't cause the failure, but duplicate detection has quietly fallen back to simple word-overlap matching instead of meaning-based similarity.

**Fixed so far (not committed):**
- **`scripts/generate-post-gemini.js`:** a 400 or 404 now skips to the next model instead of stopping the run. Bad-key errors (401/403) still stop immediately. One retired model name can no longer kill the pipeline.
- **`scripts/lib/blog-post.js`:** the embedding cache now includes the model name in its key. Without this, switching embedding models would compare vectors of different sizes and quietly give wrong duplicate scores in a local cache. CI starts with an empty cache, so it wasn't affected there. I added a regression test in `tests/lib/blog-post.test.js`; that file passes (61/61). The other two test files under `tests/lib` fail with or without my changes because the `blog-src` dependencies aren't installed here.

**What I need from you:** the Gemini API key isn't available on this machine, so I can't check which model names are valid now. The error message names `gemini-3.6-flash` but says nothing about the embedding model, and I don't want to guess. Could you run this where `GEMINI_API_KEY` is set:

```
! curl -s -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models?pageSize=200" | jq -r '.models[] | "\(.name)\t\(.supportedGenerationMethods|join(","))"'
```

With that list I'll:
- update the fallback chain in the script;
- update the embedding model default;
- update the pinned `GEMINI_MODEL` in `.github/workflows/generate-blog-post.yml`, which overrides the script's default in CI;
- check whether the `thinkingBudget: 0` setting still works on newer models. The topic picker only allows 100 output tokens, so a model that spends tokens "thinking" could return nothing.
- update the README and skill docs to match.

To confirm it really works, I'd then like to trigger the workflow once by hand in `topic` mode. Is that OK? A successful run pushes a branch and opens a real draft PR.

+# series: ""      # optional: set the same value on every part of a multi-part series

+excerpt: "In the world of high-performance networking and security, the ability to inspect and filter network traffic at the earliest possible moment is..."

+In the world of high-performance networking and security, the ability to inspect and filter network traffic at the earliest possible moment is paramount. Traditional packet filtering mechanisms, like `iptables`, while powerful, often introduce overhead and latency as packets traverse multiple layers of the kernel stack. For scenarios demanding near real-time control, such as sophisticated intrusion detection systems, custom network policy enforcement, or high-frequency trading platforms, we need a more direct approach. This is where extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) shines.

+eBPF allows us to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel itself. These programs can hook into various kernel events, including network packet reception, and execute custom logic with minimal performance impact. This post will walk you through building a custom eBPF program, compiled into a kernel module, for real-time network packet filtering. We'll focus on a practical example: dropping all incoming UDP packets destined for a specific port.
+## The Power of eBPF for Packet Filtering

+eBPF operates by allowing userspace applications to load eBPF programs into the kernel. These programs are then attached to specific "hook points." For network packet filtering, the most relevant hook points are the network ingress (`TC_INGRESS`) and egress (`TC_EGRESS`) classes within the Traffic Control (TC) subsystem. When a packet arrives at the network interface, it can be passed to an eBPF program attached to the ingress hook. This program can then inspect the packet's headers and decide its fate: permit, drop, or even redirect it.
+The key advantages of eBPF for this task are:
+*   **Performance:** eBPF programs run directly in the kernel, avoiding costly context switches between userspace and kernel space.
+*   **Flexibility:** eBPF offers a rich instruction set, allowing for complex logic and access to various packet metadata.
+*   **Safety:** eBPF programs are verified by a kernel verifier before execution, ensuring they don't crash the kernel or access unauthorized memory.
+*   **Programmability:** We can write and load custom logic without recompiling the kernel.
+## Our Goal: Dropping UDP Traffic to a Specific Port

+For this deep dive, we'll create an eBPF program that attaches to the `TC_INGRESS` hook of a network interface. This program will examine incoming packets. If a packet is UDP and its destination port matches a predefined value (e.g., 12345), the program will return an action code to drop the packet. Otherwise, it will permit the packet to continue its journey.
+We'll write our eBPF program in C, which will then be compiled into eBPF bytecode. We'll use the `libbpf` library for loading and managing the eBPF program.
+First, let's define our eBPF program. We'll need to include necessary headers and define the return codes for packet processing.
+    // Basic sanity check for Ethernet header
+        return TC_ACT_OK; // Allow if header is malformed
+    // Check if it's an IP packet (EtherType 0x0800)
+        return TC_ACT_OK; // Not an IP packet, pass through
+    // Check if it's a UDP packet (Protocol 17)
+        return TC_ACT_OK; // Not UDP, pass through
+    // Check if the destination port matches our target
+        bpf_printk("Dropping UDP packet to port %d\n", TARGET_PORT);
+// License is required for eBPF programs
+*   `#include <linux/bpf.h>` and `#include <bpf/bpf_helpers.h>`: These provide necessary eBPF types and helper functions.
+*   `#define TARGET_PORT 12345`: Defines the UDP port we want to filter.
+*   `SEC("tc_ingress")`: This macro marks the function `udp_drop_filter` as an eBPF program intended to be attached to the `TC_INGRESS` hook.
+*   `struct __sk_buff *skb`: This is the context passed to the eBPF program, representing the network packet. It contains pointers to the packet data (`data`) and its end (`data_end`).
+*   We perform checks to ensure the packet data is valid and contains the expected headers (Ethernet, IP, UDP).
+*   `bpf_ntohs(udph->dest)`: We convert the destination port from network byte order to host byte order using a helper function.
+*   `bpf_printk()`: This helper function allows us to print debug messages to the kernel's trace buffer, which can be viewed using `bpftool trace`.
+*   `TC_ACT_DROP` and `TC_ACT_OK`: These are return codes that tell the kernel what to do with the packet. `TC_ACT_DROP` discards the packet, while `TC_ACT_OK` allows it to proceed.
+*   `char _license[] SEC("license") = "GPL";`: eBPF programs require a GPL-compatible license to be loaded into the kernel.
+## Compiling and Loading the eBPF Program

+To compile this C code into eBPF bytecode, we typically use `clang` with the appropriate target architecture. We'll also need a userspace program to load this bytecode into the kernel and attach it to a network interface. The `libbpf` library simplifies this process.

+    // Set program's target port from command line argument
+    skel->btf->map_defs[0].key_size = sizeof(int); // Assuming map is for port

+    // You'd typically use a map for this, but for simplicity, we'll hardcode in C

+    // For this example, we'll rely on the C code's #define.

The blog post action should work again. I ran the full generator locally with your key and it produced a complete post. I deleted that test post afterwards. The changes aren't committed yet.

**Why it failed:** `gemini-2.5-flash` was temporarily overloaded (503), so the script tried its first fallback, `gemini-2.0-flash`. Google has retired that model and now returns a 404. The script treated the 404 as fatal and exited without trying its last fallback.

**What I changed:**
- **Fallback behaviour (`scripts/generate-post-gemini.js`):** a 400 or 404 now moves on to the next model instead of stopping the run. A bad key (401/403) still stops immediately.
- **Model list:** the chain is now `gemini-2.5-flash` → `gemini-3.6-flash` → `gemini-2.5-flash-lite`. I tested each against the live API with the script's real request settings. I kept `gemini-2.5-flash` as the primary so your posts' style doesn't change.
- **Embedding model:** `text-embedding-004` is retired, so it's now `gemini-embedding-001`. The embedding cache now includes the model name in its keys, so vectors from different models can't be compared by mistake. There's a new test for this; `tests/lib/blog-post.test.js` passes (61/61) and lint is clean.

My local run hit the free-tier quota (429) doing that, and duplicate detection fell back to simple word-overlap matching. It still works, just less precisely, and this morning's failed run had the same fallback because the old embedding model 404'd. Keeping the cache between runs (for example with `actions/cache`) would fix it. That's a separate change, which I can make if you want.

name: Generate Blog Post

on:
  schedule:
    # Daily at 8:00 AM UTC. The duplicate/mis-title problems that once
    # justified a 3x/week cadence are now caught by the pipeline's hard
    # duplicate guard, H1 title reconciliation, and the CI content tests,
    # so daily drafting is safe again.
    - cron: '0 8 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      mode:
        description: 'Generation mode'
        required: true
        default: 'auto'
        type: choice
        options:
          - auto
          - topic
          - git
      topic:
        description: 'Topic (required when mode is "topic")'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

# Avoid two scheduled runs and a manual dispatch racing each other into
# duplicate PRs against `master`.
concurrency:
  group: blog-post-generator
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  generate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      # Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs so a moved/compromised tag
      # can't inject code into a workflow that holds `contents: write`.
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # full history for git-log mode

      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Generate blog post draft
        env:
          GEMINI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GEMINI_API_KEY }}
          GEMINI_MODEL: 'gemini-2.5-flash'
          INPUT_MODE: ${{ github.event.inputs.mode || 'auto' }}
          INPUT_TOPIC: ${{ github.event.inputs.topic || '' }}
        run: |
          case "$INPUT_MODE" in
            auto|topic|git) ;;
            *) echo "Invalid mode: $INPUT_MODE" >&2; exit 1 ;;
          esac

          if [ "$INPUT_MODE" = "topic" ] && [ -n "$INPUT_TOPIC" ]; then
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js topic "$INPUT_TOPIC"
          else
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js "$INPUT_MODE"
          fi

      - name: Check for new draft
        id: check
        run: |
          if git status --porcelain | grep -q 'blog-src/src/content/posts/'; then
            DRAFT_FILE=$(git status --porcelain | grep 'blog-src/src/content/posts/' | awk '{print $2}' | head -1)
            # Title is AI-generated; never interpolate it directly into a shell command.
            # Sanitize aggressively (printable ASCII minus shell metacharacters) and cap length.
            RAW_TITLE=$(head -5 "$DRAFT_FILE" | grep '^title:' | sed 's/^title: *"//;s/"$//')
            SAFE_TITLE=$(printf '%s' "$RAW_TITLE" | tr -cd 'A-Za-z0-9 _.,:!?-' | head -c 120)
            {
              echo "has_draft=true"
              echo "draft_file=$DRAFT_FILE"
              echo "title=$SAFE_TITLE"
            } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "has_draft=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "No new draft was generated."
          fi

      - name: Create PR with draft
        if: steps.check.outputs.has_draft == 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          DRAFT_TITLE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.title }}
          DRAFT_FILE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.draft_file }}
        run: |
          DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
          SLUG=$(printf '%s' "$DRAFT_TITLE" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -cs 'a-z0-9' '-' | head -c 40)
          BRANCH="blog/draft-${DATE}-${SLUG}"

          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"

          git checkout -b "$BRANCH"
          git add blog-src/src/content/posts/
          git commit -m "draft: $DRAFT_TITLE"
          git push -u origin "$BRANCH"

          gh label create blog-draft --color "0E8A16" --description "Auto-generated blog draft" 2>/dev/null || true

          PR_BODY=$(cat <<EOF
          ## Auto-Generated Blog Draft

          **File:** \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`

          This post was automatically generated by the daily blog pipeline using Google Gemini.

          ### To publish:
          1. Review and edit the post in \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`
          2. Add appropriate tags in the frontmatter
          3. Merge this PR

          > **Note:** The post is written directly into \`posts/\`, so merging this PR
          > publishes and deploys it to the site. Close the PR without merging to discard.

          *Generated via GitHub Actions*
          EOF
          )

          gh pr create \
            --title "📝 Blog Draft: $DRAFT_TITLE" \
            --body "$PR_BODY" \
            --label "blog-draft" \
            --base master

name: Generate Blog Post

on:
  schedule:
    # Daily at 8:00 AM UTC. The duplicate/mis-title problems that once
    # justified a 3x/week cadence are now caught by the pipeline's hard
    # duplicate guard, H1 title reconciliation, and the CI content tests,
    # so daily drafting is safe again.
    - cron: '0 8 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      mode:
        description: 'Generation mode'
        required: true
        default: 'auto'
        type: choice
        options:
          - auto
          - topic
          - git
      topic:
        description: 'Topic (required when mode is "topic")'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

# Avoid two scheduled runs and a manual dispatch racing each other into
# duplicate PRs against `master`.
concurrency:
  group: blog-post-generator
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  generate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      # Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs so a moved/compromised tag
      # can't inject code into a workflow that holds `contents: write`.
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # full history for git-log mode

      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version: 22

      # Persist semantic-dedupe embeddings across runs. Without this every run
      # re-embeds every existing post and hits the free-tier embed quota (429),
      # silently degrading dedupe to lexical. Cache keys are immutable, so each
      # run saves a fresh entry and restores the newest via restore-keys.
      - name: Restore embeddings cache
        uses: actions/cache/restore@55cc8345863c7cc4c66a329aec7e433d2d1c52a9 # v6.1.0
        with:
          path: scripts/.embeddings-cache.json
          key: blog-embeddings-${{ github.run_id }}
          restore-keys: |
            blog-embeddings-

      - name: Generate blog post draft
        env:
          GEMINI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GEMINI_API_KEY }}
          GEMINI_MODEL: 'gemini-2.5-flash'
          INPUT_MODE: ${{ github.event.inputs.mode || 'auto' }}
          INPUT_TOPIC: ${{ github.event.inputs.topic || '' }}
        run: |
          case "$INPUT_MODE" in
            auto|topic|git) ;;
            *) echo "Invalid mode: $INPUT_MODE" >&2; exit 1 ;;
          esac

          if [ "$INPUT_MODE" = "topic" ] && [ -n "$INPUT_TOPIC" ]; then
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js topic "$INPUT_TOPIC"
          else
            node scripts/generate-post-gemini.js "$INPUT_MODE"
          fi

      - name: Check for new draft
        id: check
        run: |
          if git status --porcelain | grep -q 'blog-src/src/content/posts/'; then
            DRAFT_FILE=$(git status --porcelain | grep 'blog-src/src/content/posts/' | awk '{print $2}' | head -1)
            # Title is AI-generated; never interpolate it directly into a shell command.
            # Sanitize aggressively (printable ASCII minus shell metacharacters) and cap length.
            RAW_TITLE=$(head -5 "$DRAFT_FILE" | grep '^title:' | sed 's/^title: *"//;s/"$//')
            SAFE_TITLE=$(printf '%s' "$RAW_TITLE" | tr -cd 'A-Za-z0-9 _.,:!?-' | head -c 120)
            {
              echo "has_draft=true"
              echo "draft_file=$DRAFT_FILE"
              echo "title=$SAFE_TITLE"
            } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "has_draft=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "No new draft was generated."
          fi

      - name: Create PR with draft
        if: steps.check.outputs.has_draft == 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          DRAFT_TITLE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.title }}
          DRAFT_FILE: ${{ steps.check.outputs.draft_file }}
        run: |
          DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
          SLUG=$(printf '%s' "$DRAFT_TITLE" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -cs 'a-z0-9' '-' | head -c 40)
          BRANCH="blog/draft-${DATE}-${SLUG}"

          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"

          git checkout -b "$BRANCH"
          git add blog-src/src/content/posts/
          git commit -m "draft: $DRAFT_TITLE"
          git push -u origin "$BRANCH"

          gh label create blog-draft --color "0E8A16" --description "Auto-generated blog draft" 2>/dev/null || true

          PR_BODY=$(cat <<EOF
          ## Auto-Generated Blog Draft

          **File:** \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`

          This post was automatically generated by the daily blog pipeline using Google Gemini.

          ### To publish:
          1. Review and edit the post in \`${DRAFT_FILE}\`
          2. Add appropriate tags in the frontmatter
          3. Merge this PR

          > **Note:** The post is written directly into \`posts/\`, so merging this PR
          > publishes and deploys it to the site. Close the PR without merging to discard.

          *Generated via GitHub Actions*
          EOF
          )

          gh pr create \
            --title "📝 Blog Draft: $DRAFT_TITLE" \
            --body "$PR_BODY" \
            --label "blog-draft" \
            --base master

Triggers include page JS silently not running / blocked by CSP, "npm run build" or "astro check" failing on a specific post/draft, tests/site/build-output.test.ts being skipped or red, the contact form returning HTTP 403/413/415/400 or always redirecting to /contact-error/, a contact test that only fails when the whole suite runs (not alone), "Cannot find module" / import errors from tests/lib/*.test.js, scripts/generate-post*.js dying with "Could not find a sufficiently unique topic", the Lighthouse CI job failing on accessibility, or curl against the live site returning an unexpected 403/404. Covers the two-node_modules trap, the blog-src naming trap (the whole site lives there, not just the blog), workers.dev vs custom-domain probing, and the embedding-cache cold start. Do NOT use this for a settled past incident (use resumesite-failure-archaeology instead) or for measuring/benchmarking a working site (use resumesite-diagnostics-and-tooling). For the general "how do I debug anything" method, use superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then come back here for the project-specific table.

fix(blog): restore daily draft generation after Gemini model retirements

The scheduled run failed when gemini-2.5-flash returned 503 and the next

- Persist the embeddings cache across runs with actions/cache (saved
  even on failure) so runs stop re-embedding every post and hitting the
  free-tier embed quota.
- Raise job timeout to 20 minutes to fit a three-model retry chain.
EOF
git push origin master 2>&1 | tail -3; git log -1 --format='%h %s'

content.content: Monitor started (task bnpdx9iur, expires in 15m unless the source ends first; you get one notice at expiry — re-arm if you still need the watch). You will be notified on each event. Keep working — do not poll or sleep. Events may arrive while you are waiting for the user — an event is not their reply.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
